analysis.one_liner: Let shooting victims sue gun makers for damages and taxed gun sales to reimburse hospitals treating uninsured gunshot victims.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee held one hearing in June 1993, but no committee ever voted on it and it never reached the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made gun manufacturers and importers automatically financially responsible for harm caused by the handguns and assault weapons they make or bring into the country. Anyone hurt in a shooting, or the family of someone killed, could sue the gun's maker in federal court without proving the company was at fault, with a few exceptions such as injuries from police or military use. It would also have raised the federal tax on gun sales to 20 percent and used half the money to help urban hospitals cover the cost of treating gunshot victims who have no health insurance. The bill never got out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured or families of people killed by handguns or assault weapons could recover damages from the manufacturer or importer without proving the gun was defective. Urban hospitals serving uninsured gunshot victims would receive federal reimbursement, easing costs that otherwise fall on hospitals, insured patients, and local taxpayers. Taxpayers generally would not pay for the trust fund, since it came from the firearms tax itself.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shooting victims, their families, and urban hospitals

how_it_helps.text: Created a federal right for anyone injured, or the family of anyone killed, by a handgun or assault weapon to sue the weapon's manufacturer or importer for damages, without having to prove the gun was defective.
Raised the federal firearms excise tax to 20 percent and directed half the new revenue to a trust fund helping urban hospitals pay for treating gunshot victims who have no health insurance.
Required federal prosecutors, after a conviction in a federal gun crime, to tell victims or their relatives whether the new liability rule applied to the firearm used.

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers, importers, and dealers would bear the new liability exposure and a 20 percent excise tax, costs they would likely pass on to gun buyers through higher prices. Insurers backing the industry would also face new risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, importers, and gun buyers

drawbacks.text: Strict liability means manufacturers and importers could be sued for damages from a shooting without any proof of a defective product or fault on their part — a heavier standard than ordinary product liability, which critics said could effectively price guns out of the market and would likely face constitutional and industry legal challenges.

The bill raised the federal firearms excise tax to 20 percent and imposed a one-time tax on dealers' existing inventory, costs that would largely be passed on to gun buyers, including hunters and target shooters, through higher prices.

Because liability applied only to guns manufactured or imported after the law's effective date, and excluded self-inflicted injuries and injuries suffered during a felony, many real-world shootings would fall outside the law's coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — making gun makers financially responsible for the predictable harm their products cause and paying hospitals for uninsured trauma care — was real and substantial, and the tax fell on the industry and buyers rather than general taxpayers. The drawbacks are serious: strict liability without any fault or defect requirement goes beyond how product liability normally works, would likely raise gun prices, and a per-shooting suing mechanism, while potentially deterring careless marketing, is an indirect tool whose benefits are hard to guarantee. An honest supporter would acknowledge the cost was passed largely to gun buyers and the law would face court challenges; an honest critic would acknowledge the status quo left victims and public hospitals absorbing the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Ways and Means Committees, and then to their crime and tax subcommittees; after one subcommittee hearing in June 1993, no committee ever voted, so it never came to the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 2, 1993 by Rep. Mel Reynolds with 16 cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred jointly to the House Judiciary and Ways and Means Committees.
In February and May 1993 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice and the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Select Revenue Measures.
The Crime subcommittee held a hearing on June 29, 1993, but no committee or subcommittee ever voted on the bill.
No further action was taken, and the bill died at the end of the 103rd Congress in January 1995 without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers and importers are better off: they face no liability for shootings with their products and pay only the pre-existing lower excise tax.

for.name: Rep. Mel Reynolds
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured a hearing in the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice.

for.name: Rep. Don Tucker (co-introducer) and 16 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 16 cosponsors were Democrats.

for.name: National Rifle Association
for.role: Firearm industry and gun-owner advocacy group
for.what_they_did: Vigorously opposed strict liability for gun makers as part of its broader campaign against gun-liability legislation in this era.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill never attracted Republican support; no chamber vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Handgun and assault weapon manufacturers and importers
industries.note: The bill made them strictly liable for damages from shootings with their products, without any need to prove a defect, and raised the federal excise tax on their sales to 20 percent. It would have been the most significant financial exposure the industry had faced.
A new trust fund, financed by half the firearms tax revenue, would reimburse urban hospitals for treating uninsured gunshot victims — costs those hospitals and their other patients currently absorb.
Dealers would owe a one-time floor stocks tax on guns in their inventory when the higher tax took effect, and would face higher wholesale prices.
Gun purchasers would pay higher prices from the 20 percent excise tax, though the tax proceeds would help pay for trauma care that gun violence generates.
